headline: High-risk shared-filesystem and write-capability overlap can let Continue influence Dify outputs and corrupt shared workspace state.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read/write workspace files and use MCP, while Dify reads uploaded knowledge-base files and wires tools into agents. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if one agent consumes the other's file output. The pathway is not proven by docs, so I avoid higher severity, but the shared filesystem and permissive tool surfaces make injection realistic.
conditions: IF Continue writes attacker-controlled text into workspace files that Dify later ingests as knowledge-base content, injection is possible.
IF Dify agent prompts or tools treat uploaded content as instructions, the bridge becomes exploitable.
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different workspaces.
Disable automatic ingestion of newly written files into Dify.
Require provenance tags on files before Dify reads them.
Review MCP tool outputs before copying them into Dify.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation at the ingestion boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers, and Dify touches knowledge-base content and conversation logs. Both have broad network egress and filesystem access, so a shared workspace or copied artifacts could move sensitive code or logs between them. The profiles do not prove automatic exfiltration, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace directory, files can be exposed across the pair.
IF Continue or Dify uploads file contents to a model provider during normal operation, sensitive content can leave the host.
mitigations: Use separate repositories or mounted directories.
Restrict Dify uploads to non-sensitive samples.
Turn off or gate model-provider calls for sensitive sessions.
Audit logs for copied code or KB content.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation and DLP controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue has filesystem write access and Dify also has filesystem write access plus server-side Python code execution. Their concurrency models explicitly share state via filesystem or Dify datastore, so concurrent edits to the same artifacts can race and overwrite each other. Because both can mutate shared state by default, the conflict is dangerous and can cause irreversible workspace corruption.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or datastore without locking, last-writer-wins corruption can occur.
IF Dify server-side code tools modify files that Continue also edits, state divergence is likely.
mitigations: Assign disjoint write paths.
Pause one agent while the other performs writes.
Enable file locking or transactional writes.
Limit Dify code tools to read-only in shared projects.
requires-engineering: add cross-agent locking and conflict detection.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can generate code or file edits that Dify may ingest through uploaded knowledge-base files or workflow tools, and Dify's tool-wired agent model can act on that input. If Dify treats Continue's output as authoritative, mistakes or hallucinations can cascade into downstream actions or stored knowledge. The interaction is plausible in default workflows, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF Continue output is copied into Dify without verification, Dify may propagate errors.
IF Dify workflows trigger actions from imported text, a bad Continue suggestion can become an executed step.
mitigations: Require human review before importing Continue output.
Add validation steps before Dify tool execution.
Use structured schemas for exchanged artifacts.
Mark generated text as untrusted in Dify prompts.
requires-engineering: implement provenance-aware gating between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Continue handles source code, editor buffers, and model-provider API keys, while Dify handles knowledge-base content, conversation logs, and tool credentials. Their logging and retention surfaces differ, so the same sensitive material can be retained in two places with different policies. No residency mismatch is proven, but the compliance gap is credible enough for medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into both agents, retention and deletion obligations may diverge.
IF one agent logs prompts or files longer than the other, subject-rights handling can fail.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared sessions.
Align retention settings across both systems.
Document deletion/export procedures for both logs.
Review where secrets are stored and rotated.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention parity.
